title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
authors: Trieu Nguyen, Frazier N. Baker, Ruoxi Gao, Daniel Adu-Ampratwum, Xia Ning
abstract: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$).

infographic.key_insight: MFG trains an LLM to optimize molecules over multiple turns using feedback from earlier steps, improving both target properties and structural similarity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more practical drug-design pipelines by making iterative, similarity-constrained molecular optimization learnable rather than hand-crafted.
method: Reinforcement learning framework for multi-turn molecular optimization
Feedback vector encodes property gains and similarity to the source molecule
Feedback-aligned reward encourages progressive improvement across turns
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks, where GeLLM3O-MFG achieved a highest average similarity-constrained success rate of 81.50% versus 70.81% for the base model.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of the feedback signal and reward design, so noisy or biased feedback could steer optimization in the wrong direction.
infographic.paper_title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization

title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection
authors: Wenlin Zhong, Hao Wang, Kun Yuan, Fan Yang, Jinluan Yang, Dian Jin
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and $τ^2$-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.

infographic.key_insight: SkillScaffold learns when a generated skill will actually help, then injects it selectively so the agent benefits from reusable guidance without forcing unnecessary skills.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical way to reduce rollout cost and improve stability in agentic RL systems by adapting skill use to the current policy and task difficulty.
method: Reuse outcome-verified trajectories to generate candidate textual skills.
Estimate each skill’s utility via outcome-aware likelihood comparisons instead of extra environment rollouts.
Inject only helpful skills; abstain and run skill-free when no candidate is predicted to help.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improvements on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ²-Bench across both short- and long-horizon tasks, with ablations supporting utility-based selection and abstention.
infographic.watch_item: Utility estimation relies on likelihood-based proxies, so performance may depend on how well these scores correlate with real downstream skill benefit under new tasks or policies.
infographic.paper_title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection

title: Beyond the Verdict: Agentic Code Judging with Verifiable Feedback
authors: Zheye Deng, Sha Li, Changlong Yu, Xin Liu, Qin Lu, Priyanka Nigam
abstract: Test-time scaling for large language models (LLMs) can involve generating multiple candidate solutions for selection or revising an earlier attempt. To guide selection and revision, we need a verifier that can estimate candidate correctness and provide evidence of failure. In competitive programming, however, official judging systems provide authoritative verdicts under finite submission budgets, without revealing failure explanations or failing inputs. To provide informative feedback without consuming official submissions, we formulate a task in which a model judges and diagnoses a candidate program using only the problem statement and source code, with generated counterexamples serving as checkable evidence. To evaluate this task, we build USACO-JUDGE from the USACO 2026 contests, using accepted and unaccepted programs written by human experts and multiple LLMs. We then train ARBITER, a 35B mixture-of-experts (MoE) agentic verifier, with reinforcement learning in a generic execution sandbox. Training raises counterexample success on incorrect programs from 40.61% to 62.67% and mean binary verdict accuracy on USACO-JUDGE from 71.41% to 87.41%, approaching frontier verification performance. Beyond verification, ARBITER outperforms baselines in both code selection and refinement. In an IOI 2026 case study, ARBITER-guided refinement raises GPT-OSS-120B's expected score above the gold-medal threshold under the official submission limit.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns code judging from a binary verdict into an agentic verification task that also generates checkable counterexamples and failure diagnoses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for test-time scaling in competitive programming and code agents because better verification improves both candidate selection and iterative refinement under strict submission budgets.
method: Built USACO-JUDGE from USACO 2026 contest problems with accepted and unaccepted programs from human experts and multiple LLMs.
Trained ARBITER, a 35B MoE verifier, using reinforcement learning in a generic execution sandbox.
Used generated counterexamples as evidence to support verdicts and diagnosis.
infographic.evidence_signal: On USACO-JUDGE, ARBITER improved mean binary verdict accuracy from 71.41% to 87.41% and raised counterexample success on incorrect programs from 40.61% to 62.67%.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on sandboxed execution and generated counterexamples, so robustness may vary when programs are hard to trigger or when execution environments differ from official judges.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond the Verdict: Agentic Code Judging with Verifiable Feedback

title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Bowen Ding, Mingda Wan, Yuhan Chen, Jiyao Yuan, Qi Zhu, Futing Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally invalid actions in preferred trajectories and ignores the downstream cascading influence of early pivotal deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9\% and 94.3\% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7\% and 70.8\% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to $2.44\times$ while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS.

infographic.key_insight: ProAS fixes uniform trajectory-level credit assignment in critic-free LLM-agent RL by shaping advantages with a progress-aware reference graph so early, pivotal actions and invalid actions are treated differently.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a plug-and-play way to improve multi-turn agent training without adding critic overhead, making group-based RL more practical for scalable agentic systems.
method: Build a dynamic Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to track progress-aware structure across trajectories.
Apply Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) to suppress rewards for structurally invalid actions in preferred paths.
Use Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR) to spread blame more accurately for early mistakes in unpreferred trajectories.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, ProAS improved group-based baselines to new SOTA, reaching 91.9%/94.3% success on ALFWorld and 66.7%/70.8% on WebShop, while speeding convergence by up to 2.44×.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of the ARG, so imperfect or distilled graphs may reduce credit-assignment accuracy and should be validated carefully.
infographic.paper_title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning

title: Model-Based Online Decision Making via Generative Trajectory Planning
authors: Haldun Balim, Yilun Du, Na Li
abstract: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.

infographic.key_insight: Generative Trajectory Planning treats a diffusion model as a proposal distribution for action sequences, then refines sampled trajectories with learned dynamics, reward, and value models to enable efficient long-horizon planning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives practitioners a practical way to combine generative modeling with model-based control, improving trajectory-level decision making without solving a full optimization problem from scratch at every step.
method: Learn a diffusion prior over action sequences as a generative sampler.
Refine sampled trajectories using learned dynamics, reward, and value estimates.
Use the resulting candidate plans for online decision making in continuous control and manipulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that GTP matches or exceeds strong model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines on continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, with better stability in regimes where those baselines degrade.
infographic.watch_item: Performance likely depends on the quality of the learned dynamics, reward, and value models, so model error or distribution shift could reduce plan quality.
infographic.paper_title: Model-Based Online Decision Making via Generative Trajectory Planning

title: Deterministic Prediction as Global Velocity: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecast
authors: Jiajing Hu, Xu Han, Li-Ping Liu
abstract: Accurate uncertainty quantification is critical for many time series forecasting applications, and recent studies have increasingly adopted generative models to capture predictive uncertainty. Existing approaches often combine deterministic forecasting with generative modeling to improve predictive performance. However, their joint training is typically unstable because the deterministic model is embedded within the generative process, resulting in deep computational graphs and changing the probability transport path. In this work, we propose DV-Flow, a unified flow-matching formulation that incorporates the deterministic predictor as a parallel velocity component rather than as the endpoint of the transport path. This design enables stable end-to-end optimization while subsuming several existing formulations as special cases, allowing direct comparisons among them. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that DV-Flow consistently improves probabilistic forecasting performance over strong baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/tufts-ml/dv-flow-time-series.

infographic.key_insight: DV-Flow reframes deterministic forecasting as a parallel velocity in flow matching, making probabilistic time-series prediction more stable to train while preserving uncertainty modeling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives engineers a more reliable way to combine point forecasts and generative uncertainty estimates in operational forecasting systems.
method: Use a unified flow-matching objective for probabilistic forecasting.
Inject the deterministic predictor as an additional velocity component, not as the transport endpoint.
Enable end-to-end optimization while subsuming several prior formulations as special cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports extensive experiments on six real-world datasets, where DV-Flow consistently outperforms strong baselines in probabilistic forecasting.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on careful implementation of the coupled flow-matching setup and may require tuning to avoid instability in large or complex time-series models.
infographic.paper_title: Deterministic Prediction as Global Velocity: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecast

title: Self-Evolving Agent Harness
authors: Chuyang Wei, Haoxiang Guan, Minghang Zhu, Kexin Zhou, Jiyan He, Xiren Zhou
abstract: Harness self-evolution revises an agent's software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data. We examine how persistent harness revisions affect knowledge sharing and organizational workflows, with implications for scientific reliability, physical safety, and institutional accountability. Cases from prior work illustrate model--harness co-design, distributed execution, and plugin reuse. Reliable deployment requires continual validation as task distributions and evaluators change, with independent safeguards for learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. We provide a comprehensive 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, applications, and the broader impact of Harness RSI, together with continuously updated code and supplementary materials, at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.

infographic.key_insight: Self-evolving agent harnesses can improve an AI system by revising prompts, memory, workflows, and code while keeping model weights fixed, but those revisions must be admitted only through reliable validation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for building maintainable agentic systems because it enables continual adaptation of the software scaffold without retraining the base model, while adding governance for safety and accountability.
method: Formalizes a feedback-driven self-evolution loop for agent harnesses
Separates revision targets from proposal and admission mechanisms
Uses continual PAC-learning analysis to derive generalization, retention, and high-probability admission guarantees
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is primarily theoretical and survey-based, with bounds and admission rules derived under explicit assumptions plus case examples from prior work, rather than a single empirical benchmark study.
infographic.watch_item: Persistent harness changes can silently alter behavior over time, so deployment needs fresh independent validation and safeguards when task distributions, evaluators, or privileges change.
infographic.paper_title: Self-Evolving Agent Harness

title: Unlocking Token Rewards via Training-Free Reward Attribution
authors: Sitong Wu, Haoru Tan, Bin Xia, Xichen Zhang, Jingyao Li, Shaofeng Zhang
abstract: In this paper, we propose an extremely efficient, training-free method to extract token-level reward signals directly from an existing deep reward model. Our core idea is to attribute the overall process reward to individual tokens by estimating each token's influence. This influence is defined as the change in the final macroscopic reward (e.g., the process reward) when a token is replaced with a semantically null token. Naively calculating this influence is computationally infeasible, requiring N forward passes through the PRM for an N-token sequence. We overcome this bottleneck by proposing a highly efficient gradient-based estimator. Specifically, we use a first-order Taylor approximation, which simplifies the influence calculation to the inner product of the difference between the token embedding and the null token embedding, and the gradient of the reward with respect to the token embedding. This requires only a single forward and backward pass. The resulting token-level rewards enable standard RL algorithms to perform precise credit assignment without requiring additional reward model training. Experiments on challenging reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our method substantially improves policy optimization efficiency and enhances the generalization of LLM reasoning capabilities. Our P2T outperforms the outcome reward by +4.9% on MathVista for Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and +11.5% on AIME24 for Qwen2.5-Math-7B. The code will be released via https://github.com/stonewst/P2T.

infographic.key_insight: Token-level rewards can be extracted from an existing process reward model without extra training by attributing the final reward to each token via a single gradient-based pass.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables much finer credit assignment for RL training of language models, improving optimization efficiency while avoiding the cost of building a separate token reward model.
method: Define each token’s influence as the change in final reward when it is replaced by a semantically null token.
Approximate this influence with a first-order Taylor expansion using the token-embedding difference and the reward gradient.
Compute token-level rewards with one forward and one backward pass instead of N forward passes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports strong benchmark gains, including +4.9% on MathVista for Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and +11.5% on AIME24 for Qwen2.5-Math-7B.
infographic.watch_item: The approximation depends on the quality of the null-token substitution and the local linearity assumption, so attribution accuracy may degrade for highly nonlinear cases.
infographic.paper_title: Unlocking Token Rewards via Training-Free Reward Attribution

title: AIRRI: Towards a Human-Readable, Machine-Resistant Reading Interface
authors: Emory Salaun, Syed Ayon, Kaleel Mahmood, Shaun Wallace
abstract: The rapid advancement of image-to-text extraction systems and large language models (LLMs) poses new challenges for educational assessment by making assignment materials easy to transcribe and solve with minimal human effort. To address this problem, we present AIRRI (Artificial Intelligence Resilient Reading Interface), a framework for generating machine-resistant educational content, a dataset of higher-education assignments for evaluation, and an initial evaluation of the human readability of AIRRI machine-resistant text designs. AIRRI employs two categories of machine-resistance techniques. First, AIRRI applies image transformations including character spacing, word spacing, line spacing, character opacity variation, stripe overlays, and image noise. Second, AIRRI applies decision-based adversarial attacks: RayS, SurFree, and ADBA. We evaluate AIRRI against three image-to-text systems: Tesseract, EasyOCR, and the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our results show that AIRRI substantially degrades automated text extraction performance. AIRRI increased character error rates for EasyOCR (6.9% to 55.9%), Tesseract (2.3% to 100.0%), and GOT-OCR2 (30.7% to 48.1%). Word error rates increased for EasyOCR (24.9% to 96.7%) and Tesseract (10.7% to 100.0%). Among the evaluated decision-based attacks, ADBA consistently produced the largest degradation in image-to-text performance, while RayS and SurFree produced more moderate reductions. EasyOCR and Tesseract were generally more susceptible to both image-based and adversarial perturbations than the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our findings suggest that AIRRI can significantly reduce the reliability of image-to-text-to-LLM workflows, increasing the effort required for AI-assisted assignment completion.

infographic.key_insight: AIRRI makes educational text much harder for OCR and downstream LLM workflows by combining visual perturbations and adversarial attacks to reduce machine readability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a practical testbed for designing and benchmarking machine-resistant document interfaces that preserve human readability while disrupting automated extraction.
method: Applies image-based perturbations: spacing changes, opacity variation, stripe overlays, and noise.
Uses decision-based adversarial attacks: RayS, SurFree, and ADBA.
Evaluates against Tesseract, EasyOCR, and GOT-OCR2 using higher-education assignment text.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports large OCR degradation, including character error rate increases from 6.9% to 55.9% for EasyOCR and from 2.3% to 100.0% for Tesseract, with ADBA producing the strongest overall impact.
infographic.watch_item: Machine-resistant designs may trade off accessibility, visual quality, and robustness across different OCR systems, so human readability and real-world usability need careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: AIRRI: Towards a Human-Readable, Machine-Resistant Reading Interface

title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
authors: Ashutosh Hathidara
abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that an LLM agent can learn confidence signals calibrated to the eventual success of an entire multi-step episode, enabling better decide-to-act vs abstain behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for deploying agents in real systems because step-level confidence can support selective execution, human handoff, and safer long-horizon automation without reducing task success.
method: Use GRPO to train the agent’s verbalized confidence against the final episode outcome rather than the current-step correctness.
Apply a proper scoring rule to each rollout step using success labels from grouped trajectories.
Evaluate both offline on logged trajectories and online on a live ALFWorld agent, including selective execution metrics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across offline ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop evaluations, step confidence AUROC rises from near chance to 0.68–0.85, and in online ALFWorld calibration rewards reduce ECE from 0.42 to below 0.12.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest signal appears to be episode-level foresight rather than clean attempt-level discrimination, so real deployments should be cautious about over-trusting confidence on harder or early-step decisions.
infographic.paper_title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents

title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?
authors: Jason Ken Adhinarta, Raina Wu, Ashutosh Sharma, Avinash Balakrishnan, Rameswar Panda, Polina Golland
abstract: Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B-14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning

infographic.key_insight: Self-distillation does not reliably improve reasoning; the paper finds that apparent gains often come from overfitting or reusing existing behavior rather than effectively leveraging privileged information.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For practitioners building reasoning models, this suggests self-distillation should be treated as a risky optimization strategy that may not translate to robust out-of-distribution gains without stronger evaluation and reward-aligned training.
method: Revisit two self-distillation methods: SDPO and OPSD.
Test across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks.
Compare self-distillation gradients with policy gradients for reward optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors evaluate Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 14B parameters and OLMo-3-7B, finding that reported improvements do not consistently generalize to unseen problems.
infographic.watch_item: Self-distillation may look effective on in-distribution benchmarks while failing to provide a policy-improving gradient direction, so generalization and gradient alignment should be checked carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?

title: BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Xiaoguang Guo, Yaohao Long, Chuxu Zhang
abstract: Large language model multi-agent systems extend individual agents' capabilities through collaboration across specialized roles, tools, and workflows. Yet collaboration makes failures harder to diagnose: one agent may misinterpret a correct result while others carry the mistake forward. Failure attribution therefore seeks to identify the responsible agent and decisive error step. Recent methods trace dependencies, but knowing where information came from is not the same as knowing where it went wrong. We introduce BLADE (Blame Localization via Audited Dependency Evidence), a training-free framework that moves beyond tracing information to auditing its use. Using Jev for structured probabilistic judgments, BLADE uses dependency probabilities to select relevant source-decision handoffs for auditing. At these handoffs, it examines whether receiving decisions use their sources faithfully and within task requirements, distinguishing error introduction, propagation, and repair. These findings inform a global diagnosis that considers all execution steps. Without reference answers, BLADE achieves the best or tied-best step accuracy among eight strategies under a shared Jev decision interface on 1,228 failed runs across five Who&When and Who&When Pro subsets, outperforming All-at-once by 2.2-11.1 percentage points. Making responsibility evidence explicit offers a path toward more interpretable and reliable agentic systems.

infographic.key_insight: BLADE improves failure attribution in LLM multi-agent systems by auditing how information is used at key handoffs, not just tracing where it came from.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives builders a training-free way to localize responsibility in agent pipelines, making debugging and reliability analysis more interpretable.
method: Compute dependency probabilities to select source-to-decision handoffs for auditing.
Use Jev-based probabilistic judgments to check whether a receiving decision faithfully uses its source under task requirements.
Classify handoffs as error introduction, propagation, or repair, then aggregate these signals into a global diagnosis.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 1,228 failed runs across five Who&When and Who&When Pro subsets, BLADE achieved the best or tied-best step accuracy among eight strategies and beat All-at-once by 2.2-11.1 points without reference answers.
infographic.watch_item: Because it relies on probabilistic auditing of selected handoffs, performance may depend on dependency estimation quality and the reliability of the Jev judgment interface.
infographic.paper_title: BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution in LLM Multi-Agent Systems

title: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates
authors: Muyao Kong, Zhihao Lin
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the \textbf{Scenario-Actor}, which adapts decoding to the inferred situational characteristics. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines.

infographic.key_insight: Scenario-Actor adapts LLM sampling temperature from an interpretable geometric embedding of the communicative scenario, instead of using a fixed global heuristic.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical decoding control mechanism for deployment settings where output randomness should match the interaction context, improving task success without changing the base model.
method: Extract scenario-relevant structure from Transformer hidden states.
Build a structured scenario embedding that geometrically represents the communicative setting.
Map the embedding to a decoding temperature for context-adaptive generation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports strong goal-completion in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive multi-turn conversation results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct versus multiple baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on reliably inferring the scenario from hidden states, so misclassification or brittle scenario embeddings could lead to poorly tuned temperatures.
infographic.paper_title: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates

title: BridgeTwist: Twisting Schrödinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling
authors: Mengyu Li, Qianqian Qu, Jun S. Liu
abstract: Generative models are often required to serve many downstream conditional tasks. In the training-free setting, a pretrained unconditional model is reused as a prior and combined with a task-specific likelihood to sample from the corresponding posterior. While such training-free samplers have been developed for diffusion and flow models, their counterpart for Schrödinger bridge (SB) models remains unexplored, despite the growing appeal of SBs as flexible stochastic transport models between general source and target distributions. We propose BridgeTwist, a training-free conditional sampler for pretrained SB generative models, formulated as a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme. Its twist is a closed-form plug-in surrogate, obtained by combining the velocity and score fields exposed by SB pretraining into an endpoint predictor and evaluating the likelihood there. Since this surrogate is less reliable near the source, we temper the twist with a time-varying exponent, downweighting its influence at early steps. We further introduce a bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule that concentrates the proposal noise in the interior of the path. Telescoping importance weights then cancel all intermediate twist factors, yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior. Empirically, BridgeTwist outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and is competitive with specialized inverse problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.

infographic.key_insight: BridgeTwist turns a pretrained Schrödinger bridge into a training-free conditional sampler by twisting the bridge with a likelihood-based surrogate and time-varying tempering.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a reusable inference-time way to adapt one generative model to many downstream conditional tasks without retraining.
method: Builds a plug-in twist from the SB velocity and score fields to predict endpoints and score the task likelihood there.
Uses a time-varying exponent to weaken the twist near the source where the surrogate is least reliable.
Adds a bridge-shaped diffusion schedule and importance weighting so intermediate twist factors telescope away.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method is evaluated on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and on inverse problems including inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution, where it outperforms training-free baselines and is competitive with specialized solvers.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of the endpoint surrogate and the chosen tempering/schedule, especially early in the bridge where the twist is least accurate.
infographic.paper_title: BridgeTwist: Twisting Schrödinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling

title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization
authors: Yangchengyu Zhou, Zhiping Wu, Runchang Jiang, Dongdong Ren, Youfang Han, Wei Zhao
abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference. Extensive experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks demonstrate that MultiAlloc consistently improves over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods under matched memory budgets across diverse models, including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.

infographic.key_insight: MultiAlloc allocates a fixed KV-cache memory budget across layer-wise precision and token-wise preservation to improve quantization quality without online search.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a practical, profiling-driven way to reduce LLM inference memory while preserving accuracy for long-context and reasoning workloads.
method: Lightweight offline profiling measures layer sensitivity and token importance.
The profiler estimates the memory–accuracy trade-off under a fixed budget.
An allocation policy is derived once and applied during inference, avoiding online search.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent gains over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV-cache quantization methods on reasoning and long-context benchmarks across Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on offline profiling being representative of the target model and workload, so mismatches in deployment data could reduce gains.
infographic.paper_title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization

title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
authors: Mattie Ji, Indradyumna Roy, Vikas Garg
abstract: Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows how to generate graphs whose persistent homology matches a target persistence diagram exactly, rather than only approximately.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables topology-constrained graph generation for scientific and engineering workflows where strict structural guarantees matter.
method: Local method: iteratively build degree-based PD-equivalent graphs using implicit topological constraints.
Global method: encode exact PD matching as a complete constraint-satisfaction problem solvable with modern CP solvers.
Supports any vertex-based permutation-equivariant filtration and is minimal under degree filtration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks show both proposed methods realize the target persistence diagram exactly.
infographic.watch_item: The local approach can trade off diversity and may get trapped in infeasible states, so solver-based scalability and practicality should be checked for larger graphs.
infographic.paper_title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs

title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
authors: Bingxin Xu, Wenrui Bao, Xinxin Liu, Jiawei Zhou, Yuzhang Shang, Emilio Ferrara
abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.

infographic.key_insight: ChunkAct reduces redundant LLM reasoning in agentic robotics by grouping routine primitives into autonomous action chunks, so the planner is invoked only when new decisions are needed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This shifts control from per-primitive planning to decision-level planning, cutting inference cost and latency while preserving generalization to unseen tasks.
method: Compile robot memory into executable action chunks offline.
Launch a chunk with one LLM call; let primitives chain autonomously until failure.
Reserve LLM reasoning for sub-goal selection and exception handling.
infographic.evidence_signal: On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over prior agentic robotics methods while using 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on how well memory can be compiled into reliable chunks; failures inside a chunk still require robust exception detection and recovery.
infographic.paper_title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics

title: Joint Neural Posterior Estimation and Model Selection for Chemical Reaction Networks
authors: J. Arturo Esquivel, Jorge A. Campos-Gonzalez-Angulo, Sergio Pablo-García, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Vianey Leos-Barajas
abstract: Simulation-based Bayesian inference for Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) must simultaneously solve two computationally demanding problems: discriminating between overlapping reaction pathways and estimating reaction rate constants. Classical approaches, such as Sequential Monte Carlo ABC, rely on handcrafted summary statistics and scale poorly across large parameter spaces. To overcome this, we introduce a neural inference architecture. Our pipeline utilizes shared 1D-CNNs and a permutation-invariant Set Attention mechanism to learn low-dimensional summary statistics from variable-length, multi-experiment time-series data. These statistics simultaneously condition a model selection network to compute posterior model probabilities and model-specific conditional Invertible Neural Networks (cINNs) that estimate parameter posterior distributions. We demonstrate the practical utility of our approach on a real protodeboronation example, illustrating how it handles structural ambiguity and extracts kinetic parameters from competing catalyst deactivation pathways.

infographic.key_insight: The paper presents a unified neural inference pipeline that jointly chooses the most plausible chemical reaction network and estimates its kinetic parameters from time-series experiments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, more scalable simulation-based inference for reaction engineering problems where multiple mechanisms fit the same data.
method: Shared 1D-CNNs learn compact features from variable-length time-series experiments.
A permutation-invariant Set Attention module aggregates multi-experiment information into low-dimensional summaries.
These summaries feed a model-selection network plus model-specific conditional INNs for posterior parameter estimation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation on a real protodeboronation case, showing the method can resolve competing catalyst deactivation pathways and recover kinetic parameters.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the quality and diversity of simulated training data, and the added model-selection step can be sensitive when candidate mechanisms are highly similar.
infographic.paper_title: Joint Neural Posterior Estimation and Model Selection for Chemical Reaction Networks

title: Tiny Recursive Message Passing
authors: Tommaso Salvatori, Matteo Forasassi, Alexis Toumi, Giovanni de Felice
abstract: Message passing neural networks have shown remarkable performance in algorithmic and constraint reasoning, due to their ability to encode the structure of the task directly in the architecture. Recent work has shown that better results can be achieved using recursive transformers trained with deep supervision and truncated recursions, which make extremely deep loops stable to train, and equipped with test-time procedures such as discrete deduction lattices. In this work, we apply the same procedures to message passing networks, and show that the two ingredients are complementary, and lead to parameter efficient models: we obtain about $99\%$ test accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme with a model of $16$k parameters that trains in about $10$ minutes on an H100, or in $9$ hours on a CPU. We further show that the cost of truncating gradients grows with the number of rounds information needs to cross the graph, making the choice of wiring a trade-off between robustness to truncation and transfer across problem sizes. We conclude by showing that our models transfer zero-shot to larger instances than those seen during training, outperforming popular neural baselines on N-queens and Boolean satisfiability with a fraction of their parameters.

infographic.key_insight: Tiny recursive message passing combines recursive training tricks from transformers with message passing networks to achieve high-accuracy reasoning on algorithmic tasks with very few parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach suggests a practical path to compact, fast-to-train models for constraint solving and structured reasoning, especially when compute and parameter budget are limited.
method: Apply deep supervision to train very deep recurrent/recursive message passing loops.
Use truncated backpropagation through time to stabilize optimization while keeping the model small.
Add test-time discrete deduction lattice procedures to improve reasoning performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports about 99% test accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme with a 16k-parameter model, plus zero-shot transfer to larger N-queens and SAT instances.
infographic.watch_item: Truncating gradients can hurt more when information must travel across many graph rounds, so wiring and graph diameter must be chosen carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Tiny Recursive Message Passing

title: Brain Age Gap Progression in Individuals at Risk for Neurodegeneration
authors: Jason Scheffel, Saurabh Sihag
abstract: Neuroimaging is a widely used modality for characterizing neurodegeneration in various health conditions. Brain age gap has emerged as a promising biomarker for monitoring brain health from neuroimaging data using machine learning algorithms. Recent studies have leveraged coVariance neural networks (VNN)-driven pipelines based on the advancements in graph signal processing for relatively transparent construction of brain age gap from neuroimaging data. In this paper, we focus on a longitudinal study of VNN-based brain age gap in conjunction with Alzheimer's Progression Score (APS) in individuals that are at a higher risk of neurodegeneration due to family history of Alzheimer's disease. APS is a multimodal marker of disease progression. The longitudinal analysis of APS and VNN-derived brain age gap metrics revealed that a higher risk of disease progression at baseline predicted a larger rate of increase in brain age gap in follow-up visits. Thus, our findings revealed potential stratification in the brain age gap modulated by clinical/biological risks of AD in the at-risk population.

infographic.key_insight: In people at elevated risk for neurodegeneration, a higher baseline Alzheimer's Progression Score predicted a faster increase in VNN-derived brain age gap over follow-up.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests longitudinal brain-age models can be used to stratify risk and monitor progression using neuroimaging plus clinical biomarkers.
method: Used a coVariance neural network (VNN) pipeline to estimate brain age gap from neuroimaging data.
Combined brain age gap with Alzheimer's Progression Score (APS) in a longitudinal analysis.
Compared follow-up changes in brain age gap against baseline disease-risk/progression status.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a longitudinal study in a family-history-at-risk cohort, finding that higher baseline progression risk was associated with a larger subsequent increase in brain age gap.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report cohort size, external validation, or effect sizes, so generalizability and clinical readiness remain uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Brain Age Gap Progression in Individuals at Risk for Neurodegeneration
